Title: [from] “To Make It to the Moon, Women Have to Escape Earth's Gender Bias”
Author: by Mary Robinette Kowal
Content: As we celebrate the `50^text(th)` anniversary of the Apollo `11` moon landing, NASA has started Artemis, a program that aims “to return astronauts to the lunar surface by `2024`, including the `text(first)` woman and the next man.”

Although both astronauts have enormous challenges ahead, the `text(first)` woman will face added hurdles simply because everything in space carries the legacy of Apollo. It was designed by men, for men.

Not deliberately for men, perhaps, but women were not allowed in the astronaut program until the `text(late 1970s)`, and none flew until Sally Ride became the `text(first)` American woman in space, in `1983`. By this point, the space program was built around male bodies.

If we do not acknowledge the gender bias of the early space program, it becomes difficult to move past it. `text(One)` of the most compelling things about NASA is its approach to failure. Failure is not penalized in its culture; it is valued for the things that it can teach to save lives or resources in the future. As Bobak Ferdowsi, a systems engineer at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory has said, “our best mistakes are the `text(ones)` we can learn from.”
What are the lessons to be learned from NASA's failure to fly women during the Apollo era?

The most recent lesson emerged in `text(April)`, when NASA had scheduled a spacewalk that was, quite by accident, staffed by `text(two)` female astronauts. The agency had to restaff the spacewalk because it had only `text(one)` spacesuit that was the correct size for both women.
This is not an indictment of NASA in `2019`. But it does demonstrate a causal chain that begins with the Apollo program and leads through to present-day staffing choices.

The suits, known as extravehicular mobility units, were designed more than `text(40 years)` ago, based on the designs of the Apollo missions, at a time when all astronauts were men. Only `text(four)` of the original `18` suits are still rated for spaceflight, and all of those are on the space station.

NASA `text(first)` planned to have extra-small, small, medium, large and extra-large suits. For budget reasons, the extra-small, small and extra-large suits were cut. However, many of the male astronauts could not fit into the large suits, so the bigger size was brought back.

Cady Coleman, an astronaut who has flown on `text(two)` space shuttles and traveled to the space station, stands `text(5 feet 4 inches)` tall and remains the smallest person to ever qualify for a spacewalk. While she was training in NASA's Neutral Buoyancy Lab, she had to improvise padding to wear inside her spacesuit.

Without that, smaller people would have an air bubble inside their suits that would make them spin in the lab's pool as if a beach ball were strapped to their stomachs. It would not be a problem in space, Ms. Coleman told me. “But the N.B.L. was where people decided if you had what it takes to do a spacewalk,” she said.

And complaints? Well, no one else previously had that problem, so it must just be the person who complained. As a result, this gender bias became a mistake that we did not learn from, because the female astronauts compensated.
